name: Buddha Jayanti at Lumbini
when: Full moon of Baisakh, usually late April or May
summary: The Buddha's birthday, celebrated on the full moon of Baisakh at the place where he was born. Monks and pilgrims from across Asia gather at the Sacred Garden for chanting, processions and offerings, and Hindu villagers come to worship Maya Devi as Rupa Devi.
body: In Nepal the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death are all remembered on one day, the full moon of the month of Baisakh, called Buddha Jayanti or Buddha Purnima. It is a national holiday, and nowhere is it marked more fully than at Lumbini, his birthplace.

From dawn the Sacred Garden fills with monks and nuns in saffron, maroon and grey from Nepal, Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Tibet, Japan and Korea. There are processions along the central canal, chanting at the Maya Devi temple and the Ashoka pillar, butter lamps and flowers around the Puskarini pond, and ceremonies at many of the monasteries in the monastic zone.

Lumbini's festival is not only Buddhist. Many Hindus regard the Buddha as an incarnation of Vishnu, and villagers from the surrounding plains come on the same full moon to worship Maya Devi as Rupa Devi, the mother goddess of the place. Expect heat, crowds and a remarkable mix of people.
tips: Arrive at the Sacred Garden at first light, before the heat and the largest crowds.
Book rooms in Lumbini months ahead; hotels fill with pilgrim groups.
Carry water, a hat and a light scarf; temperatures in late April and May often pass 38 °C.

faqs.q: When is Buddha Jayanti celebrated in Lumbini?
faqs.a: Buddha Jayanti falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Baisakh, usually in late April or May. The exact date follows the lunar calendar and changes each year. In Nepal it is a public holiday, and Lumbini holds the main national celebrations. Check current status before you travel for the year's date and programme.

faqs.q: What happens at Lumbini on Buddha Jayanti?
faqs.a: Monks, nuns and pilgrims gather at the Sacred Garden for chanting, processions, offerings of flowers and butter lamps, and prayers at the Maya Devi temple and the Ashoka pillar. Monasteries in the monastic zone hold their own ceremonies, and official events are often held with national leaders and foreign guests.

faqs.q: Is Lumbini very crowded on Buddha Jayanti?
faqs.a: Yes. Lumbini receives large numbers of pilgrims from Nepal, India and across Asia on Buddha Jayanti, and security is tighter than usual. The Sacred Garden is busiest from mid-morning. Hotels fill early, so book well ahead and plan your temple visit for dawn.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists join Buddha Jayanti celebrations?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of any faith are welcome to watch and take part respectfully. Dress modestly, remove shoes at temples, keep quiet during chanting and ask before photographing monks and pilgrims at prayer. Many Hindu families also attend, worshipping Maya Devi as Rupa Devi.

name: Ridi Mela at Maghe Sankranti
image_query: Ridi Mela Maghe Sankranti Kali Gandaki
when: Mid-January, from Maghe Sankranti (Magh 1), for three days
summary: A three-day bathing fair at Ridi, where the Ridi Khola meets the Kali Gandaki, starting on Maghe Sankranti in mid-January. Pilgrims bathe at dawn, worship at the Rishikesh temple and fill the old bazaar with stalls of chaku, yam and sesame sweets.
body: Maghe Sankranti, the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, marks the sun's turn northwards and the end of the coldest part of winter. Across Nepal families eat ghee, chaku, sesame laddu, yam and sweet potato. At Ridi, one of the holiest confluences in the western hills, it brings the biggest fair of the year.

The fair lasts three days, known as Jethi, Maili and Kanchhi Sankranti, the eldest, middle and youngest. Devotees believe that bathing in the Kali Gandaki on all three days and worshipping at the Rishikesh temple brings liberation. Before dawn the ghats are crowded with families stepping into the cold river and praying towards the rising sun.

By day the bazaar becomes a market for the whole region. Traders from Gulmi, Palpa, Syangja, Arghakhanchi and Baglung sell food, cloth, tools and household goods, and families picnic on the riverbank. It is loud, crowded and one of the best chances to see hill Nepal celebrating together.
tips: Stay in Tansen and leave by 4 am, or arrange a room in Ridi months in advance; lodges fill completely.
Wear warm layers for the dawn bath and quick-drying clothes if you plan to step into the river.
Keep valuables close and agree a meeting point with your group in the crowds.

faqs.a: The Ridi Mela begins on Maghe Sankranti, the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, which usually falls on 14 or 15 January, and lasts three days. Dates follow the Nepali calendar and shift slightly each year, so check current status before you travel and plan transport early.

faqs.q: Why do people bathe at Ridi on Maghe Sankranti?
faqs.a: Ridi is a confluence on the sacred Kali Gandaki, and Maghe Sankranti marks the sun's northward turn, an auspicious time for purification. Devotees believe bathing here over the three days of the fair and worshipping at the Rishikesh temple removes sins and helps the soul towards liberation.

faqs.q: What food is eaten at Maghe Sankranti?
faqs.a: Maghe Sankranti foods include chaku, a hard molasses toffee, sesame laddu, ghee, boiled yam called tarul, sweet potato and spinach. They are thought to warm the body in winter. At Ridi, stalls along the bazaar sell chaku, laddu and tarul by weight throughout the fair.

faqs.q: How do I get to Ridi for the mela?
faqs.a: Ridi is about 2 hours by road from Tansen. Extra buses run during the fair, but roads jam and parking fills early, so we recommend a private jeep leaving Tansen well before dawn, or staying in Ridi itself if you can book a lodge months in advance.

name: Bhagwati Jatra, Tansen
when: The day after Krishna Janmashtami, late August or early September
summary: Tansen's biggest festival, also called Sindoor Jatra: the chariot of the goddess Rana Ujeshwori Bhagwati is pulled through the steep streets amid clouds of vermilion, remembering Palpa's part in the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–16. It has been held since about 1820.
body: The Rana Ujeshwori Bhagwati temple stands by the Tansen Durbar square. It was built by Ujir Singh Thapa, Palpa's commander, as an offering to the goddess after Nepali forces held off the British East India Company in the Anglo-Nepalese War. The festival has been celebrated every year since 1877 in the Nepali calendar, about 1820 CE.

On the day after Krishna Janmashtami, the image of the goddess is placed in a wooden chariot and pulled through the town's lanes. Crowds throw sindoor, red vermilion powder, until the streets, the chariot and everyone near it are red, which is why many call it Sindoor Jatra. Music, drums and the shouts of the chariot pullers echo between the old Newar houses.
It falls in the monsoon, so expect rain and slippery lanes, but the festival shows Tansen at its fullest: families returning home, shops closed, and the whole town in the streets.
tips: Wear old clothes and cover your camera; vermilion powder stains and gets everywhere.
Book a room early, as families and visitors from across Palpa fill Tansen's hotels.
Watch from a doorway or balcony when the chariot climbs steep lanes; the crowd surges at those points.

faqs.q: When is Bhagwati Jatra in Tansen?
faqs.a: Bhagwati Jatra is held on the day after Krishna Janmashtami, which usually falls in late August or early September. The date follows the lunar calendar and changes every year, so check current status before you travel. It falls in the monsoon, so expect rain.

faqs.q: Why is it called Sindoor Jatra?
faqs.a: Sindoor is the red vermilion powder used in Hindu worship. During the festival crowds throw it over the goddess's chariot, each other and the streets, turning everything red. Because of this, many people in Palpa call the festival Sindoor Jatra.

faqs.q: What is the history of Tansen's Bhagwati Jatra?
faqs.a: The festival honours the goddess Rana Ujeshwori Bhagwati, whose temple was built by the Palpa commander Ujir Singh Thapa after Nepal's resistance to the British East India Company in the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–16. The jatra has been celebrated since 1877 in the Nepali calendar, around 1820 CE.

faqs.q: Is Bhagwati Jatra suitable for tourists?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are welcome, and it is one of the best ways to see Tansen's community life. Expect crowds, vermilion powder, steep wet lanes and loud music. Keep cameras protected, wear shoes with grip and stay out of the chariot's path on slopes. Families with small children should watch from a safe spot.
